===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Design and build a complex, production-shaped native iOS app that requires a
real server-side backend (not local-only, not a static/offline app) — pick a
genuinely creative, non-obvious idea that solves a real, specific pain point
well enough that it has a real shot at organic/viral growth. Do not default
to another todo-list, habit-tracker, journaling, or AI-wrapper app — those
categories are saturated and none of them are "unique." Think harder for an
underserved, emotionally sticky, inherently-social-or-real-time problem
where a mobile client + backend architecture is actually necessary (real-time
sync across users/devices, a shared/live data feed, matching or coordination
between people, server-side processing too heavy for on-device, etc.) — the
backend requirement should come from the idea being genuinely multi-user or
real-time, not be bolted on.

Requirements for the idea itself (spend real effort on this — the idea is
the deliverable, not just the code):
- Solves one specific, sharply-defined pain point for a specific audience
  (not "everyone"). Be able to state the pain point and audience in one
  sentence each.
- Has a natural viral/sharing loop baked into the core mechanic — not a
  bolted-on "invite friends" button, but something where using the app is
  inherently more valuable or fun with other people, or naturally produces
  something worth sharing outside the app.
- Genuinely requires a backend: real-time multiplayer/sync, a live shared
  feed, server-side matching/aggregation, push notifications driven by
  server-side events, or similar — justify the architecture choice.
- Is creative enough that a stranger hearing the one-line pitch would say
  "oh that's clever" rather than "isn't that just [existing app]?"

Technical scope:
- Native iOS client (SwiftUI).
- A real backend service (your choice of stack — pick something sensible
  and justify it) handling auth, data sync/storage, and whatever real-time
  or server-side logic the concept needs.
- Design the API contract, data model, and sync/real-time strategy properly
  before building — this is a "complicated app," not an MVP toy.
- Production-shaped: reasonable auth flow, error handling, loading/empty/
  offline states, and a coherent onboarding funnel a real user could follow.
- Visual design should be distinctive and match the concept — not generic
  default SwiftUI styling — but the primary bar for this app is the idea,
  the architecture, and it actually working end-to-end (client <-> backend).

Start by proposing and committing to the specific concept (pain point,
audience, viral loop, and why it needs a backend) before moving into specs
and build, and carry that concept consistently through naming, design, and
onboarding copy.

## Final Output

This phase confirms: **single-app build, no portfolio split.** The prompt asked for one native iOS app, and the concept that emerged from prompt_contract and product_research — a trust-graph-restricted, real-time pickup-relay coordination app for a school pickup pod — is inherently one app, not a decomposable set of sibling apps.

Selected app:
- **slug:** `pulse-relay`
- **category:** real-time trust-graph coordination / social-utility (explicitly not marketplace, not generic messaging, not "matching")
- **promise:** When a parent can't make pickup, their pod knows within seconds and exactly one person locks it in — no double coverage, no guessing who saw the message.
- **target user:** A parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod (one classroom/carpool cluster) hit by an unplanned same-day pickup conflict.
- **build:** true

Rejected alternatives: splitting into sibling apps (separate requester/helper apps, a pod-admin companion app, a group-chat clone, a caregiver marketplace, a generic emergency-alert app); generic todo/habit/journal/AI-wrapper reskins; single-user-only designs; open stranger/proximity matching; daycare/activity pod variants in v1; location-tracking-first designs. `portfolio_json` is null — this is not a portfolio parent.

Build-priority guidance carried into later phases: if build time is constrained, cut breadth in secondary screens (pod management, profile/settings polish) before ever compromising the correctness or speed of the two locked core funnels (post relay request → pod visibility; accept → conflict-resolve → complete), since the core loop's trustworthiness is the entire value proposition.

{"phase": "initial_discussion", "one_paragraph_summary": "The initial_discussion phase locked a single, mutually-confirmed product definition for pulse-relay across two rounds. Product promise: a parent in a school-pickup pod broadcasts a same-day pickup coverage need and exactly one trusted pod member locks it in via a server-arbitrated first-accept-wins mechanism, with no ambiguity and no silent failure states. Primary user: a parent/guardian of a child under 13 in a specific, pre-existing school-pickup pod, acting one-handed under real time pressure with roughly ninety seconds of attention. The core loop was locked with explicit named states end-to-end: post request (no child PII) -> live pod visibility + push deep-link -> accept -> server-arbitrated first-accept-wins -> confirmed/already-covered states -> optional release/reopen -> optional time-aware still-open escalation with re-broadcast -> complete -> combined audit/receipt record. Two failure-mode requirements were elevated to core-loop, non-secondary status: acceptance is reversible until handoff completion, with an explicit release action that reopens the request and re-notifies the pod (~30s target), because an unretractable 'confirmed' state manufactures dangerous false certainty; and an unfulfilled request must show a visible, time-aware 'still open' state (not silence or a static pending label), because silent ambiguity on an actually-open request is an equally dangerous failure mode. The data model was required to support multiple simultaneously-open requests per pod (not a single-active-request assumption), even if the UI leads with a focused single card. ===== DECISIONS LOG (structured, authoritative) =====
- [DEC-prompt_contract-001] The deliverable is a single native SwiftUI iOS app with a real backend — no portfolio/multi-app interpretation.
  rationale: Prompt uses singular 'app' throughout with no quantity language.
  rejected: Building multiple small concept apps to hedge risk
  constraints: Later phases must not split scope into multiple unrelated apps
- [DEC-prompt_contract-002] Todo lists, habit trackers, journaling apps, and AI-wrapper apps are banned as the core offering, including disguised reskins of them.
  rationale: Explicitly forbidden in the prompt; reskins would violate the spirit even if not the letter.
  rejected: Allowing a reskinned habit tracker with social features bolted on
  constraints: A candidate concept must be checked against this list before being accepted
- [DEC-prompt_contract-003] Production-readiness is defined by checkable behaviors, not aesthetics: real empty/loading/error states verified under airplane mode and on a fresh zero-state account, session persistence across force-quit, and no UI claiming Saved/Synced/Sent without real backend acknowledgment.
  rationale: Prevents 'production-shaped' from being quietly redefined down to 'compiles and has a login screen'; matches this factory's recorded history of placeholder/blank-screen failures.
  rejected: Treating production-readiness as a subjective/aesthetic judgment call
  constraints: Every stateful screen must expose all four states before any later phase can claim it done
- [DEC-prompt_contract-004] The backend requirement must be provably load-bearing: the core value must fail or degrade for a solo user on one device with no second account/device involved.
  rationale: Prevents a bolted-on Firebase/API call from satisfying 'genuinely requires a backend' while the real experience is single-player.
  rejected: Accepting any app with a network call as satisfying the backend requirement
  constraints: Verification must include a live two-account/two-device test, not just an API existing
- [DEC-prompt_contract-005] The care-and-handoff relay concept for parents/guardians is carried forward as the working concept, provisionally, not as an immutable lock — it proceeds subject to a rollback gate if it fails the two-device/backend-load-bearing test or the safety constraints below.
  rationale: Resolves the round-1 phase-boundary disagreement: Codex wanted to commit now, Claude wanted concept-commitment treated as a distinct later step; both agreed a provisional-but-testable commitment satisfies both concerns.
  rejected: Treating the concept as fully and finally locked in this phase with no further challenge; Deferring all concept discussion to a separate phase with no candidate carried forward
  constraints: Any later phase must be able to reject or revise this concept if it fails the load-bearing backend test or safety constraints; Rollback must be explicit and documented if the concept is abandoned
- [DEC-prompt_contract-006] Matching is restricted to a pre-established trust graph (existing contacts, or verified members of a school/daycare pod a parent explicitly joins) — never open proximity-matching with unknown strangers.
  rationale: Removes the core safety liability of algorithmically pairing a child handoff with an unvetted stranger, while preserving every backend-necessity argument (live availability, real-time acceptance, capacity/routing logic).
  rejected: Open proximity-based matching with nearby unknown users; Leaving matching scope unspecified and deciding it ad hoc during build
  constraints: Data model and matching logic must enforce trust-graph/pod membership as a hard filter, not a ranking signal
- [DEC-prompt_contract-007] No UI element may imply identity verification, background-check completion, or safety vetting that the app does not actually perform; self-reported or peer-vouched trust must be labeled plainly as such.
  rationale: Prevents a decorative 'Verified' badge or trust score from being mistaken for real vetting in a context (child handoff) where that mistake is dangerous, not just misleading.
  rejected: Using unqualified 'Verified Guardian' badges based only on self-reported profile fields
  constraints: Design review and copy review must check every trust-related UI element against this rule before it ships
- [DEC-prompt_contract-008] Proof that a real backend endpoint is deployed and reachable from the iOS client is required as the first deliverable of the next (architecture/build) phase, before any concept-specific schema or screens are trusted as real.
  rationale: Both participants agreed 'genuinely requires a backend' is meaningless if reachability is never actually confirmed in this build environment; discovering this at final verification would be too late.
  rejected: Assuming backend reachability and confirming it only at final verification
  constraints: No feature-specific screen work should be considered validated until this reachability proof exists
- [DEC-prompt_contract-009] Naming and pitch framing must lead with the trust-graph/pod mechanic, not generic 'matching' language.
  rationale: Leading with 'matching' makes the pitch sound like derivative 'Uber for childcare,' which is both less clever and more alarming than the actual trust-graph-constrained mechanic.
  rejected: Pitching the app primarily around real-time matching/availability without foregrounding the pod/trust-graph structure
  constraints: Onboarding copy, app name, and marketing-style pitch language must foreground pod/trust-graph membership as the distinctive mechanic

**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 1**

Pulse Relay should be built for one specific audience: parents or guardians of children under 13 who belong to a known school-pickup pod and occasionally lose pickup continuity at the last minute. The pain point is not general family coordination; it is the exact failure where a parent asks “who got my child?” in real time and the existing group thread gives multiple “I can do it” responses, silent ambiguity, or no one taking ownership.

The app exists because that moment is high-stakes and emotionally expensive: group chats are too ambiguous, and emergency services / taxi apps are wrong products for a trust-graph-only handoff. A real-time relay with explicit server-side claim arbitration and a single source of truth prevents duplicate coverage and removes uncertainty, which is a materially different outcome from messaging.

The core loop is: compose and post a same-day request with one tap and optional short note; pod members receive push that deep-links directly to the live request card; first person to accept gets a locked claim via server arbitration; everyone else sees “already covered by X” in seconds; if the accepter must drop out, they release and the request reopens instantly with re-notify; if no one accepts, the card escalates with visible elapsed-time “still open” status and explicit re-broadcast; once handoff is completed, the app writes one trust-relevant artifact that is both internal audit evidence and a shareable privacy-filtered receipt without child PII. States must be visible and explicit at every step, and nothing can show “accepted/completed/synced” until backend-acknowledged.

Paid value is the reduction of real uncertainty: parents pay for a faster, safer pickup response and for accountability that group chat can never provide. The first subscription unlock should not be cosmetic; it should unlock utility: stronger pod-scale reliability and operational comfort. A viable model is family + pod capacity based on team needs (for example, larger pods with more than one child group per day), durable receipt retention and export windows, advanced escalation policies (auto-repeat windows and fallback channels after X minutes), and response-time analytics for parents and pods that want to improve coordination. In v1, this can be documented as phased product direction while shipping the free utility loop first, because the current constraints require no in-app payments during first build.

The competitive wedge is being a deterministic relay infrastructure instead of yet another parent thread: no maps-first experience, no stranger matching, no payments, no recurring task engine, no chat bloat. The differentiator is the trust-graph primitive plus load-bearing server logic (single-winner claim, explicit release, explicit still-open escalation, and audit/receipt integrity). The product’s trust claim is narrow and honest: “you coordinate with known pod members,” never “verified” in ways the system does not provide.

Viral or niche growth is inherent in how the value is consumed, not bolted on: a pod is the launch mechanism. The same event that makes one parent safer also makes the pod more useful for everyone in that school micro-network. Receipt sharing stays minimal and privacy-safe (proof-of-coverage text/card for spouse/partner/school staff only), not a social feed, so growth stays tied to real-world usage rather than vanity interactions. Network growth occurs because pods solve repeated pain quickly and spread through existing parent-school trust circles.

Local-first behavior should be deterministic and calm: offline compose works as a draft queue, local cache shows last known request/feed state, and the app keeps readable context (who requested what, elapsed time, current state) during intermittent connectivity. Cloud is required for truth: acceptance arbitration, live fanout, push fan-in/out, and audit artifact generation must be server-side. A safe bridge is local persistence + sync reconciliation, where local actions are queued, then atomically reconciled with backend state and updated with clear conflict/error messaging.

The biggest risk is social overreach into false confidence: users must never infer guarantees (real-time safety or background checks) that are not true. The non-negotiable detail this phase must preserve is the explicit state machine discipline: claimed, already-covered, reopened, still-open, and error states are always visible, and backend acknowledgment is the only trigger for success messages. ### Round 2


**Codex (Design Lead · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

Codex, I’m with the core lock and I think the subscription story is the one place we still need hard edges, because if we get this wrong the whole trust architecture gets undermined by business logic. I agree with your broader read that this is a reliability product, but “pod reliability / capacity tiers / analytics” is too broad for a first paid thesis unless we define what each unlocks without touching safety-critical behavior. Claude’s tighter list is the right direction because it keeps the paid layer honest: free must always include every core relay action (request, accept, release, complete, audit artifact) for at least one pod, forever.

The one real user is still exactly what we already converged on: a parent or guardian already in a named school pickup pod, under real-time pressure, who rarely uses the app daily but must be fully confident in one moment when things break down. The reason this app exists is not “another coordination tool”; it fixes a specific failure mode no group chat can solve: uncertainty under stress caused by multiple simultaneous “I can do it” replies, silent drops, and no machine-checked owner.

Core loop to keep in copy and in UX should stay this deterministic sequence and no other: post a same-day request with one short note and no child PII; pod members get a deep-linked push; first server-confirmed accept locks it; all other concurrent accepts resolve to explicit already-covered; any accepter can release up to handoff completion, which reopens and re-notifies in under ~30 seconds; unresolved requests don’t disappear or sit in generic pending—they show elapsed time and still-open state with re-broadcast; completion writes one object that is both audit record and privacy-filtered shareable receipt. This is exactly why the app deserves to exist: it turns shared text ambiguity into a source of truth with visible state, and that reduces wrong assumptions in a safety-adjacent moment.

For subscription value, I’d lock to three unlocks only: multi-pod seats for households spread across multiple schools or pods, exportable signed receipt bundles for custody/co-parenting/legal handoff proof, and critical-alert notification priority (for example bypass DND with explicit consent) for families who want stronger interruption guarantees. Everything else in this phase stays free, including any number of requests and all first-pod usage. That keeps moral and product risk low and gives a clear “you pay for utility breadth, not for basic safety.”

Competitive wedge is still clean if we describe it honestly: Pulse Relay is not a marketplace, not stranger matching, not location dispatch, and not chat; it’s a trust-graph relay layer that enforces one accepted owner with server-side arbitration and a full state machine (confirmed / already-covered / reopened / still-open / error) so people don’t self-interpret noise as truth. That’s fundamentally different from WhatsApp-style pickup coordination or Life360-like surveillance workflows.

The growth mechanism should be explicit that it is not a vanity-share loop: the receipt card exists as a proof artifact, not a trigger for users to “share to build virality.” Real growth is trust compounding within the same social unit—after a first successful first-rescue event, someone pastes a natural sentence in the existing class chat (“this app worked and got someone assigned in 40 seconds”), and the pod recruits by lived proof, not by app-level social features. So the design constraint is social but non-viral: optimize for near-zero-friction first use, because one broken first incident on a new pod likely ends adoption.

Local-first should be narrowly strong: immediate render from cache for context and read flows, explicit offline draft state for compose actions, and strict server acknowledgment gating for any outcome-affecting action. No optimistic “confirmed,” no local false positive on accept. Cloud-ready path is straightforward: the request/audit graph is already server-authoritative, so phase-2 can add pod-type polymorphism and household multi-identity without changing v1 data primitives. What keeps users: speed plus correctness on the first incident, visible no-silence states, and the certainty that the app never tells them “done” until it’s actually done.

**Claude (QA & Risk · Closer) — Round 2**

Codex, let's actually resolve this instead of both restating our positions past each other. Your subscription list — "pod-scale reliability," capacity tiers, escalation policies, response-time analytics — sounds reasonable in the abstract, but walk through what "pod-scale reliability" or "capacity tiers" would literally mean as a paywall in this specific app. A pod is a fixed group of families in one classroom. There's no meaningful sense in which a paying pod gets more "capacity" than a free pod — the whole architecture already has to support every pod having multiple simultaneous open requests, per DEC-initial_discussion-006, for free, because that's a correctness requirement not a premium feature. If "capacity" isn't gated on the free tier for safety reasons, then what exactly would a paid capacity tier be selling? I think that item doesn't survive contact with our own locked requirements. Same problem with "advanced escalation policies (auto-repeat windows and fallback channels after X minutes)" — the still-open escalation state and re-broadcast path are core-loop requirements from initial_discussion (DEC-initial_discussion-005), not secondary polish, so if auto-repeat timing becomes a paid knob, we've just gated a safety behavior behind a subscription, which is exactly the trust failure I flagged and you didn't push back on. I'll take your silence on that specific point as tacit agreement, but I want it said out loud and locked, not left as an unstated assumption: nothing that touches the state machine (claimed/already-covered/reopened/still-open/error) can ever have a free-tier-degraded version. That has to be an explicit constraint in this phase's output, not something the architecture phase infers.

Response-time analytics is the one item on your list I think is actually defensible, but not as a v1 subscription feature — it's a real thing (a pod admin or curious parent wanting to see "average response time: 4 min" for their pod), but it's squarely a nice-to-have that adds a whole new screen and a new server-side aggregation job for a use case nobody in this room has actually argued a parent would pay for, versus my three items which each map to a concrete person with a concrete unmet need I can name: the two-school parent, the co-parenting parent who needs documentation, the parent who has their phone on Focus during work hours and needs pickup pings to break through. I'd rather we commit to shipping exactly those three and explicitly deferring analytics and escalation-policy customization to "not in this build," the same way we deferred pod-admin consoles and daycare pod types. Vague "phased product direction" is how scope quietly expands later — I want a closed list.

On growth: you're framing the receipt card as a real part of the loop and I don't think that's wrong, I think it's just secondary and I want to make sure it doesn't get built as if it were the primary mechanic, because that would be a real misallocation of build time. Here's the concrete failure mode if we get this backwards: if the team spends effort polishing the shareable receipt card's visual design as "the growth feature," while the underlying accept-race-condition or notification latency has any rough edges, we get a pretty card that nobody ever sees because the pod's first real incident went badly and everyone quietly went back to the group chat. The receipt card literally cannot fire until after a successful complete — it's a lagging artifact of things having already gone right, not a lever that makes things go right. So I'll restate this as the thing I want locked, not just argued: the growth mechanic is unglamorous and has no UI of its own — it's "the core loop has to work flawlessly on the first real incident for every new pod," full stop, and the receipt card is a nice secondary sharing surface that supports that but isn't the mechanism. If anyone downstream reads this brief and starts designing an "invite your pod" screen or a referral flow as the growth feature, that's a sign this got lost in translation, and I want that sentence to survive verbatim into the final output.

Last thing, and I think this one's actually already agreed and just needs to be stated as a decision rather than left implicit: no optimistic accept confirmation, full stop. Codex's message described local persistence plus "atomic reconciliation with backend state," which is compatible with what I said but doesn't explicitly rule out an optimistic UI flash before the reconciliation completes — and given that the entire product's reason to exist is "confirmed means confirmed," I want zero ambiguity here. The UI shows a distinct "sending/awaiting confirmation" state between tap and server ack, never a premature "you've got it," even for a fraction of a second, even to make the tap feel responsive. That's worth the minor UX cost of a barely-perceptible delay indicator, because the opposite failure — a UI that visually confirms before the server has actually arbitrated the race — is precisely the bug this whole app exists to prevent group chats from having.

So, to close this out concretely: three subscription unlocks only (multi-pod membership, exportable receipt/audit history, critical-alert notification tier), explicit free-tier-never-gates-the-core-loop-or-state-machine rule, growth mechanic named as first-incident reliability with the receipt card as secondary support not the primary lever, and no optimistic accept-confirmation UI anywhere in the client. I think that's a brief the next phase can build from without more debate.

## Final Output

**Target user & pain point:** A parent/guardian already belonging to one specific, named school-pickup pod (one classroom/carpool cluster), who uses the app rarely — a handful of times a semester — but needs total confidence in the moment a same-day pickup conflict hits and the class group chat's "I got it!" replies collide or go silent.

**Why it deserves to exist:** It replaces an unreliable social protocol (a group chat where multiple people can claim coverage at once, or nobody claims it and nobody notices) with a machine-arbitrated source of truth: exactly one accepted owner, enforced server-side, always in a visible, named state (claimed / already-covered / reopened / still-open / error) — never silence, never simultaneous false confirmation.

**Core loop (unchanged, restated as final):** post same-day request (no child PII, optional short note) → live to pod + deep-linked push → first server-confirmed accept locks it → all other concurrent accepts resolve to explicit "already covered" → accepter can release any time up to handoff, which reopens and re-notifies in <~30s → unresolved requests show elapsed time and a "still open" re-broadcast path, never a static pending state → completion writes one object that's simultaneously the audit record and the privacy-filtered shareable receipt.

**Subscription value — locked to exactly three unlocks, nothing else in v1:**
1. Multi-pod membership (for a parent with kids at two schools, or a primary + backup pod).
2. Exportable/signed receipt-and-audit history (PDF/CSV) for custody or co-parenting documentation needs.
3. Critical-alert-tier notifications that can interrupt Focus/DND.

Response-time analytics and any escalation-policy customization are explicitly deferred, not built in v1 — they're real ideas but don't map to a concrete paying user the way the three locked items do, and analytics in particular would require new server-side aggregation for an unvalidated need.

**Hard rule (new, explicit):** the free tier includes every core relay action — post, accept, release, complete, and the resulting audit/receipt artifact — fully and forever for at least one pod. Nothing that touches the state machine (claimed/already-covered/reopened/still-open/error) may ever be degraded, delayed, or gated behind payment. Paid tiers sell breadth of utility across pods/households, never basic safety.

**Competitive wedge:** not a chat thread (no simultaneous-claim ambiguity), not Life360-style location surveillance, not a caregiver marketplace or stranger-matching service, not a fake-verification trust badge — a trust-graph relay layer with real server-arbitrated single ownership.

**Growth mechanic (locked, no dedicated UI):** growth is not a feature — it's a direct consequence of the core loop working flawlessly on every new pod's first real incident. The shareable receipt card is a secondary proof artifact that supports word-of-mouth after a successful save; it is not the growth lever and should not be over-invested in relative to core-loop reliability. If a later phase starts designing an "invite your pod" or referral screen as *the* growth feature, that's a signal this brief got lost in translation.

**Local-first / cloud-ready:** reads render instantly from local cache (last known request/pod state); writes that change outcome state (accept, release, complete) always show an explicit "sending / awaiting confirmation" transitional state and never an optimistic success flash — confirmed means the server has actually confirmed, with zero exceptions, even for a fraction of a second. Compose actions taken offline sit in an explicit "will send once connected" draft state. Cloud is the sole source of truth for arbitration, fan-out, and audit-artifact generation. Deferred cloud-ready extensions (not built now): additional pod types as config on the existing pod entity, multi-guardian identity per household, and pod-health/response-time analytics as a pure server-side aggregation.

For idempotency, I want a named test case sitting right next to the two-phone race demo in the acceptance bar: force-quit the app mid-accept (after tap, before ack), relaunch, and confirm the client reconciles from the server rather than trusting whatever local state it died in — Codex, your risk register covers "lost network during race" with awaiting-confirmation-plus-timeout, which is close but isn't quite the same failure as a killed process losing all client-side state entirely; I think it needs its own line. And on the audit record surviving account deletion — since neither of us has contradicted the "persists with a deleted-user placeholder" framing, and it directly follows from why we built the export feature (a co-parent shouldn't be able to unilaterally erase the other party's documentation), I want to just call that locked unless you object.

One more gap in your risk register I want to add explicitly: nothing in it covers spam or bad-faith posting. Since v1 deliberately has zero pod-admin capability beyond create-and-invite (no member removal, per DEC-initial_discussion-007), there's no way to stop a bad actor inside a pod from repeatedly posting fake or joke "urgent" requests, and every post is free and unlimited. I'm not proposing we build moderation now — that would blow the scope we've spent five phases narrowing — but I think this needs to be written down as an accepted v1 limitation the same way cold-start and Focus/DND are, rather than silently discovered later. Codex, your no-cancel instinct is the right safety concern in spirit, but without an explicit “no longer needed” terminal action, you’re not preventing harm—you’re just delaying it until expiry. The stale-open case can burn real people the same way a false acceptance does. So I’m ready to keep your underlying principle (don’t create a misleading “completed” state) and split the meaning cleanly: this is **not** “cancel” or “handoff complete,” it is a **request termination** signal.

Here’s the concrete fix: add a first-class `withdrawn` terminal state in v1 for `open`/`still-open`/`reopened` requests, callable only by the requester. It’s the server-authoritative equivalent of “I don’t need this now.” It should only be allowed while no one has validly claimed the request (`state in {open, still_open}` and `claimedBy == null`). If someone wins the race while a withdraw is in flight, CAS decides deterministically; the loser gets whichever is true. When withdrawn, everyone gets a push/refresh event (“Requester withdrew this request; no coverage needed”) and it must never generate a receipt/audit artifact. This is exactly the anti-false-confidence control the app needs for real-world safety, and it is different from `complete`.

For visibility and trust, I also want to reject any “soft” treatment: `withdrawn` must be a distinct terminal UI and copy, not folded into success/error/pending. Think of the same style bar as `already covered by …`: fast clarity, not ambiguity. So I’m signing it as a real state machine object: openness is about “is it still active,” not “is help guaranteed.” This also makes “accepted = claimed responsibility, not guaranteed arrival” still true and enforceable.

On your spam point: I think we should lock this as an explicit V1 limitation, not pretend it’s solved. We can’t add moderation without undoing the minimal-surface decisions we’ve already made (no pod admin screen, no removal flows), but we *can* make abuse non-mysterious. So decision: “No in-app moderation / no report-or-remove in v1; any fake posting is still possible by existing members.” Mitigation is transparent identity+auditability (every request always attributable to a member), creator-only code revoke/reissue, and explicit onboarding/help copy that this is a trust-graph, invitation-based tool for known pods—not a public platform. That keeps the promise clean: strong guarantees where possible, explicit limits where not.

In short: `withdrawn` gets added, spam abuse remains a documented v1 boundary, and both are architecture-facing, non-negotiable now so we don’t quietly drift into a safer-sounding but unsafe implementation.

I'll hold my ground on withdrawn/no-longer-needed, but let me actually engage with the specific fear Codex raised instead of just restating my position, because I think there's a real kernel of truth in it that a better design can absorb rather than a flat no.

Codex's worry, as I read it, is that a cancel-type action introduces ambiguity under stress — the panicking parent doesn't know if tapping it undoes someone else's acceptance, or means something different than it looks like. That's a legitimate UX risk, but notice it's actually an argument for designing the withdrawn state carefully, not for omitting it entirely. Here's the thing that resolves it: withdrawn should only be offered to the requester while the request is still in the `open`/`still-open` state — the moment someone accepts it, the requester's screen shows "already handled by [name]," and the withdraw action simply isn't there anymore, because there's nothing to withdraw; the accepter would use release instead, which we've already locked as a distinct action. So there's no ambiguity about undoing someone else's commitment, because the two actions live in mutually exclusive states and only ever one of them is even visible to a given user at a given time. On the "will this be misread" question, I'd make it visually impossible to confuse with completion: withdrawn shows as a muted/gray closed card labeled "Withdrawn — no longer needed," structurally distinct from the green "Complete" receipt-generating state, and — this is the part that actually addresses Codex's underlying worry about trust-trail confusion — a withdrawn request generates *no* audit/receipt object at all, since nothing happened. I'd like to just call this resolved on my side: withdrawn state ships, gated to the open/still-open window only, zero audit artifact, distinct visual treatment, active re-notify on withdrawal. ## Final Output

This phase resolves the concrete edge cases that stress-test the already-locked pulse-relay core loop, without changing scope:

- **Notification honesty**: the app tells the truth about what it actually knows — "Sent to N pod members" based on real push-token/registration status, with a warning banner if delivery looks uncertain. This is a documented, accepted free-tier limitation, not a bug to chase.
- **Time/date handling**: all same-day cutoffs and elapsed-time/aging math are computed server-side in UTC against a pod-home-timezone set at pod creation — no client-local-time logic anywhere in this path.
- **Idempotency**: every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) carries a client-generated action ID; the server handles duplicates idempotently; a relaunch after a crash always reconciles from server truth. A force-quit-mid-accept-before-ack test is added as a named check alongside the two-phone race demo.
- **Join-code security**: the pod-creator role gains exactly one new capability — revoke-and-reissue the join code — as a narrow safety escape hatch, not a reopening of the admin console that was cut earlier.
- **Pod-of-one state**: a brand-new pod with no other members gets its own empty state and CTA ("share invite"), distinct from "pod has members but no response yet" (re-broadcast/escalate).
- **Audit record persistence**: the audit/receipt object outlives either party deleting their account; the departed party renders as a placeholder so neither side can unilaterally erase shared documentation.
- **"Accepted" semantics**: UI copy explicitly states accepted means "a trusted member claimed responsibility," never "help is guaranteed to arrive."
- **New `withdrawn` state**: a requester-only terminal state, usable only while a request is still open/still-open/reopened and unclaimed, arbitrated through the same CAS path as accept, that produces a real push re-notify but never an audit/receipt artifact, and is visually/semantically distinct from `complete`. It's mutually exclusive with `release` by construction — only one of the two actions is ever visible to a given user at a given time, so there's no ambiguity about undoing someone else's commitment.
- **Spam/bad-faith posting**: named and accepted as a v1 limitation. No moderation, reporting, muting, or member removal ships in v1; the only mitigations are trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution, and the new code revoke/reissue capability. This is explicit, not implied, and is revisited only if real abuse surfaces.

Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

Phase rules:
- Enumerate edge cases before features expand.

- Convert open questions into assumptions or explicit exclusions.

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

The product_research phase concluded with the concept reframed as a 'micro-supply network for immediate care continuity' — coordinating a temporary trust transfer among people who already know each other (a specific school pickup pod), not a marketplace or matching app. The real incumbent identified is the plain class WhatsApp/GroupMe thread, whose gaps (no live acceptance state, no de-duplication of simultaneous 'I got it' replies, no accountability record) justify the backend requirement. Comparable patterns (Life360, ClassDojo/Brightwheel, Nextdoor, HopSkipDrive, Uber/Lyft) were named as ASSUMPTIONs to calibrate what to avoid: map-centric design, open-board social-discovery feel, and paid/background-checked trust models rejected in the prior phase. The team locked a narrow first-build scope: exactly one pod type (school pickup only, no daycare/activity in v1), no GPS/live location, no child PII (names/photos), and an invite-link or admin-issued pod-join-code flow with a real empty state so onboarding doesn't dead-end for users without an existing pod. The accept-flow race condition was elevated to a named, testable first-build acceptance criterion: server-side first-accept-wins via conditional/compare-and-swap update, an explicit 'already claimed' state for the losing acceptor, sub-30-second propagation target, and a required two-device concurrent-accept test case. The audit/evidence log and the shareable 'relay receipt' viral artifact were merged into a single underlying data object with two views — an internal audit record and a privacy-filtered shareable summary card — satisfying both the safety/audit requirement and the growth mechanic with one data model decision. **Must-have interactions:**
- Explicit "sending / awaiting confirmation" transitional state on every outcome-affecting tap (post, accept, release, complete) — never an optimistic success flash.

- The race-loss "already covered by [name]" transition is treated as critical-path UX, not optional polish — it must read as clear, relief-inducing resolution, not as an error or malfunction, and is prioritized ahead of every other visual element in this slice, including the receipt card.

- Release/reopen re-notifies the pod within the ~30-second target.
- Force-quit and relaunch preserves auth session and the current request/feed state.

**Codex (Product Strategist · Visionary) — Round 3**

Claude, I agree with your “wrong-action in good faith” example, and it’s exactly the gap I want to close now. Codex, your no-cancel instinct is the right safety concern in spirit, but without an explicit “no longer needed” terminal action, you’re not preventing harm—you’re just delaying it until expiry. The stale-open case can burn real people the same way a false acceptance does. So I’m ready to keep your underlying principle (don’t create a misleading “completed” state) and split the meaning cleanly: this is **not** “cancel” or “handoff complete,” it is a **request termination** signal.

Here’s the concrete fix: add a first-class `withdrawn` terminal state in v1 for `open`/`still-open`/`reopened` requests, callable only by the requester. It’s the server-authoritative equivalent of “I don’t need this now.” It should only be allowed while no one has validly claimed the request (`state in {open, still_open}` and `claimedBy == null`). If someone wins the race while a withdraw is in flight, CAS decides deterministically; the loser gets whichever is true. When withdrawn, everyone gets a push/refresh event (“Requester withdrew this request; no coverage needed”) and it must never generate a receipt/audit artifact. This is exactly the anti-false-confidence control the app needs for real-world safety, and it is different from `complete`.

For visibility and trust, I also want to reject any “soft” treatment: `withdrawn` must be a distinct terminal UI and copy, not folded into success/error/pending. Think of the same style bar as `already covered by …`: fast clarity, not ambiguity. So I’m signing it as a real state machine object: openness is about “is it still active,” not “is help guaranteed.” This also makes “accepted = claimed responsibility, not guaranteed arrival” still true and enforceable.

On your spam point: I think we should lock this as an explicit V1 limitation, not pretend it’s solved. We can’t add moderation without undoing the minimal-surface decisions we’ve already made (no pod admin screen, no removal flows), but we *can* make abuse non-mysterious. So decision: “No in-app moderation / no report-or-remove in v1; any fake posting is still possible by existing members.” Mitigation is transparent identity+auditability (every request always attributable to a member), creator-only code revoke/reissue, and explicit onboarding/help copy that this is a trust-graph, invitation-based tool for known pods—not a public platform. That keeps the promise clean: strong guarantees where possible, explicit limits where not.

In short: `withdrawn` gets added, spam abuse remains a documented v1 boundary, and both are architecture-facing, non-negotiable now so we don’t quietly drift into a safer-sounding but unsafe implementation.

## Final Output

This phase resolves the concrete edge cases that stress-test the already-locked pulse-relay core loop, without changing scope:

- **Notification honesty**: the app tells the truth about what it actually knows — "Sent to N pod members" based on real push-token/registration status, with a warning banner if delivery looks uncertain. This is a documented, accepted free-tier limitation, not a bug to chase.
- **Time/date handling**: all same-day cutoffs and elapsed-time/aging math are computed server-side in UTC against a pod-home-timezone set at pod creation — no client-local-time logic anywhere in this path.
- **Idempotency**: every outcome-affecting action (post/accept/release/complete/withdraw) carries a client-generated action ID; the server handles duplicates idempotently; a relaunch after a crash always reconciles from server truth. A force-quit-mid-accept-before-ack test is added as a named check alongside the two-phone race demo.
- **Join-code security**: the pod-creator role gains exactly one new capability — revoke-and-reissue the join code — as a narrow safety escape hatch, not a reopening of the admin console that was cut earlier.
- **Pod-of-one state**: a brand-new pod with no other members gets its own empty state and CTA ("share invite"), distinct from "pod has members but no response yet" (re-broadcast/escalate).
- **Audit record persistence**: the audit/receipt object outlives either party deleting their account; the departed party renders as a placeholder so neither side can unilaterally erase shared documentation.
- **"Accepted" semantics**: UI copy explicitly states accepted means "a trusted member claimed responsibility," never "help is guaranteed to arrive."
- **New `withdrawn` state**: a requester-only terminal state, usable only while a request is still open/still-open/reopened and unclaimed, arbitrated through the same CAS path as accept, that produces a real push re-notify but never an audit/receipt artifact, and is visually/semantically distinct from `complete`. It's mutually exclusive with `release` by construction — only one of the two actions is ever visible to a given user at a given time, so there's no ambiguity about undoing someone else's commitment.
- **Spam/bad-faith posting**: named and accepted as a v1 limitation. No moderation, reporting, muting, or member removal ships in v1; the only mitigations are trust-graph invite-only membership, per-request attribution, and the new code revoke/reissue capability. This is explicit, not implied, and is revisited only if real abuse surfaces.

Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

----- Testing And Quality -----
# Testing & Quality for a Small iOS App

Target: **iOS 17+ deployment / Swift 5.9+**, built with **Xcode 16 or later** (Swift Testing ships in-box; use `OS=latest` in CI so the simulator version tracks your toolchain). Zero third-party deps — everything here is Apple first-party. This is a pragmatic reference for an AI building a prototype: maximize confidence per line of test code, avoid brittle tests that break on every UI tweak.

---

## TL;DR strategy for a prototype

- **Don't chase coverage.** Test the code that would be embarrassing or expensive if wrong: money math, date logic, parsing, persistence round-trips, state machines, reducers/view models.
- **Skip testing SwiftUI view bodies.** Use **Xcode Previews** as your visual feedback loop instead — they are faster than any UI test.
- **Make logic testable by moving it out of views** into plain `struct`/`class` types with injected dependencies. If it's testable, it's usually also better architected.
- **One happy-path UI test** through the primary flow catches wiring/regression bugs that unit tests can't. More than a handful of UI tests is usually a net negative for a prototype (slow, flaky).
- **Prefer Swift Testing (`@Test`)** for new unit tests. Keep XCTest for **UI tests** (`XCUIApplication`) and **performance tests** (`measure`) — those APIs are XCTest-only.

Priority order to write tests, highest first:
1. Pure logic with branches (pricing, validation, formatting, sorting/filtering).
2. View model / reducer state transitions (given input → expected observable state).
3. Persistence & serialization round-trips (Codable, SwiftData/UserDefaults).
4. Networking mappers (raw JSON → domain model), with a fake session — never hit the real network.
5. One end-to-end UI smoke test of the core flow.

---

## Project setup

- **Unit test target**: File ▸ New ▸ Target ▸ *Unit Testing Bundle*. Choose **Swift Testing** (default in Xcode 16+) or XCTest.
- **UI test target**: separate *UI Testing Bundle* — it launches the app as a black box.
- Add app code to tests with `@testable import YourApp` (unit tests only; gives access to `internal` symbols). UI tests use the accessibility layer, not imports.
- A `.xctestplan` lets you group tests, set env vars, and pick run configurations (e.g. randomized order). One default plan is fine for a prototype.
- Swift Testing and XCTest **coexist in the same target and same run** — migrate incrementally.

---

## Swift Testing (`@Test`) — the modern default

Import `Testing`, not `XCTest`. Tests are global functions or methods annotated `@Test`; assertions use `#expect` (non-fatal, keeps going) and `#require` (fatal, unwraps/stops).

```swift
import Testing
@testable import MyApp

@Test func totalIncludesTax() {
    let cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10), .init(price: 5)])
    #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0.1) == 16.5)
}
```

- `#expect(expr)` records a failure and **continues** — the macro captures sub-expression values, so a failure prints the actual operands (no need for XCTest-style messages).
- `#require(expr)` throws and **halts the test** on failure — use it for preconditions where continuing is pointless. It also unwraps optionals (call in a `throws` test with `try`):

```swift
@Test func parsesUser() throws {
    let user = try #require(User(json: validJSON))  // stops here if nil
    #expect(user.name == "Ada")
}
```

### Suites and shared setup

Group with a `struct` (preferred) or `final class`. A **fresh instance is created per test**, so `init` is your per-test setup — no shared mutable state between tests by default.

```swift
@Suite("Cart pricing")
struct CartTests {
    let cart: Cart              // built fresh for every @Test below

    init() { cart = Cart(items: [.init(price: 10)]) }

    @Test func emptyTaxIsIdentity() {
        #expect(cart.total(taxRate: 0) == 10)
    }
}
```

Teardown: for a `struct` suite there usually is none — value types just drop when the instance goes away. If you genuinely need cleanup, use a `final class` and put it in `deinit`. Note `deinit` **cannot be `async` or `throwing`** and can't be actor-isolated, so for `@MainActor` suites or async cleanup, do the work at the end of each test (or use a custom scoping trait) rather than relying on `deinit`.

### Parameterized tests — one test, many cases

Replaces copy-pasted test bodies. Each argument runs as a **separate, independently-reported case**. A single array of tuples destructures positionally into multiple parameters:

```swift
@Test(arguments: [
    ("", false),
    ("a@b.co", true),
    ("no-at", false),
])
func validatesEmail(_ input: String, _ expected: Bool) {
    #expect(EmailValidator.isValid(input) == expected)
}
```

Destructuring is positional — element labels in the tuples don't have to match parameter names and are best omitted to avoid confusion. Cross-product of two sequences (every combination):

```swift
@Test(arguments: [1, 2, 3], ["x", "y"])   // 6 cases
func combos(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(!s.isEmpty && n > 0) }
```

Wrap in `zip(a, b)` when you want **paired** (not cross-product) cases:

```swift
@Test(arguments: zip([1, 2, 3], ["a", "b", "c"]))   // 3 cases
func paired(n: Int, s: String) { #expect(n > 0 && !s.isEmpty) }
```

### Traits: naming, tagging, skipping, known bugs

```swift
@Test("Discount never goes negative")                       // display name
@Test(.disabled("flaky until CI fix"))                      // skip, stays visible
@Test(.enabled(if: FeatureFlags.checkoutV2))                // conditional run
@Test(.bug("https://example.com/issue/42", "rounding"))     // url first, then title
@Test(.tags(.fast))                                         // group across files
```

Define tags once (do **not** add `@Test` — a tag is not a test):

```swift
extension Tag { @Tag static var fast: Self }
```

Run a subset from the CLI with `swift test --filter` / `xcodebuild ... -only-testing:`, or filter by tag in Xcode's Test navigator.
